b: Revelation is a vision given to John, written to seven real churches in the Roman province of Asia under pressure to compromise with idolatry and the worship of the emperor. In a symbolic language drawn mostly from the Old Testament, it pulls back the curtain: God is on the throne, the Lamb who was slain has already won, evil will be judged, and those who stay faithful will share his victory. Read it for its message rather than as a coded timetable.
It ends where the Bible began: the last two chapters answer the first two of Genesis. A garden becomes a city, the tree of life returns, the curse is gone, and God lives with his people face to face.

hist.t: How to read Revelation: four approaches
b: Revelation is an ‘apocalypse’ (a revealing), a prophecy (1:3) and a letter to seven real churches (1:4), all at once. It is written in symbols drawn mostly from the Old Testament: beasts, horns, numbers, colours. Christians have read it in four main ways, and many combine them.

Preterist (from Latin for ‘past’): most of the book describes events of John’s own time, such as Roman persecution or the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. Its strength: it gives the book meaning for its first readers. Its weakness: the book calls itself prophecy, and some of it (chapters 21–22) is plainly still future. Historicist: the book maps out church history from John’s day to Christ’s return. Most of the Reformers read it this way and identified the beast with the papacy; Wesley did too. Its weakness: its followers have never agreed which events the visions describe. Futurist: from chapter 4 on, the book describes events still to come just before Christ’s return. It takes the predictive element seriously; but it is hard to see what most of the book would have meant to its first readers. Idealist: the book pictures the timeless struggle between God and evil, and calls believers in every age to endure. It catches the book’s pastoral purpose, but the book does claim to speak of real future events.

The New Bible Dictionary concludes that ‘None of the views has proved completely satisfying’ and that a true view probably combines elements of all four. Many evangelical scholars today read it that way: rooted in the first century, relevant to every age, and moving towards a real, future return of Christ.

b: The author calls himself John (1:1, 4, 9; 22:8), a servant of God, a prophet and the readers’ brother, exiled on Patmos. In the 2nd century Justin Martyr (about AD 150) and Irenaeus (about AD 180) identified him as John the apostle, son of Zebedee. In the 3rd century Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, argued that its Greek was so different from John’s Gospel that it must be by another John. Most critical scholars today agree with Dionysius and think of a Christian prophet named John who knew the churches of Asia well.

The case for the apostle. The earliest witnesses, Justin and Irenaeus, name him; Irenaeus had known Polycarp, John’s disciple. The author needs no title: he simply calls himself ‘John’, as if everyone in the churches of Asia would know which John. The Greek is unusual, but that may reflect the apocalyptic style, heavy use of Hebrew idioms, and perhaps writing without a secretary’s help in exile. And there are links with the Gospel: both call Jesus ‘the Word’ of God (John 1:1; Revelation 19:13) and ‘the Lamb’, and both quote Zechariah 12:10 about ‘those who pierced Him’ (John 19:37; Revelation 1:7). Some scholars (for example E. Stauffer) hold that one author wrote all five Johannine books.

b: About AD 95, under Domitian, is the view of most scholars today. Irenaeus says the vision ‘was seen no very long time since, but almost in our day, towards the end of Domitian’s reign’, and Eusebius agrees. The letters to the churches suggest communities that had existed long enough to grow complacent (Ephesus, Sardis, Laodicea), and Laodicea is rich again after the earthquake of AD 60.

About AD 68–69, just after Nero, was widely held in the 19th century and still has able defenders, notably Kenneth Gentry (Before Jerusalem Fell, 1988), who credits his teacher Greg Bahnsen with convincing him of it. They count the ‘seven kings’ of 17:10 from the first emperors, making the sixth (‘one is’) Nero or one of his short-lived successors, and they note that 11:1–2 seems to treat the temple in Jerusalem as still standing. Preterist readers usually prefer this date.

hist.t: Emperor worship in the province of Asia
b: The cities John writes to competed for the honour of building temples to the emperors. Pergamum had a temple of Rome and Augustus; Smyrna won the right, over rival cities, to build a temple to Tiberius; Ephesus acquired its first imperial temple under Domitian. The Roman historian Suetonius says Domitian dictated a letter beginning ‘Our Master and our God bids that this be done’, ‘And so the custom arose of henceforth addressing him in no other way’.

Pressure on Christians was often economic and social rather than official. Trade guilds held meals and sacrifices in honour of patron gods, and probably of the emperor. A believer who refused could lose his livelihood (compare ‘no one could buy or sell’, 13:17). Under Nero, the Christians of Rome had already been put to death in large numbers in AD 64: Tacitus says some ‘were covered with wild beasts’ skins and torn to death by dogs; or they were fastened on crosses’. Revelation tells such believers that the one on the throne is God, not Caesar, and that the Lamb has already won.

b: By AD 200 Revelation was accepted as Scripture by Melito of Sardis, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria and Tertullian. But some doubted it: Gaius of Rome (about AD 210) rejected it, Dionysius of Alexandria questioned its author, and in the 4th century Eusebius listed it among the ‘disputed’ books. It was slow to be accepted in the Greek-speaking East and is still not read in the Eastern Orthodox liturgy, though it is part of their Bible. By the Middle Ages it was accepted almost everywhere.

1.t: The word means unveiling. A blessing is pronounced on the one who reads it aloud and those who hear — it was written to be read in church.
John describes him with Daniel's phrase for the son of man, and then with Daniel's description of the Ancient of Days. Note the titles at verse 17: the First and the Last.

2.t: Real churches with specific problems. The pattern is consistent: what he knows, what is wrong, what to do, and a promise to the one who conquers.

3.t: Lukewarm, in a city with a famously tepid water supply. The image is not half-hearted versus zealous but useless versus useful. He stands at the door and knocks — addressed to a church, not to unbelievers.

4.t: Before any judgement, a throne room. The structure matters: whatever follows, this is the fixed point.

5.t: John hears of a Lion and turns to see a slain Lamb. The reversal is the theological centre of the book. Every creature then worships the one on the throne and the Lamb together.

6.t: Conquest, war, famine, death — and under the altar, the question 'how long'. Revelation does not pretend that history is comfortable. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

7.t: From every nation, tribe, people and language — the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham. God will wipe away every tear.

12.t: A retelling of the whole conflict in symbol. The dragon is identified plainly at verse 9, and he is defeated by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony.

13.t: Political and religious power in league. The number is most persuasively read as a coded reference to Nero, whose name in Hebrew letters totals 666, though other readings exist. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

19.h: The rider on the white horse
19.t: The return, in warfare imagery — but note that his robe is dipped in blood before the battle begins, and the weapon is a sword from his mouth.

20.t: The passage that divides millennial views. Amillennial, premillennial and postmillennial readings have all been held by serious Christians. None of them should be made a test of fellowship. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

20.h: How to hold a passage like this
20.t: Christians who agree on everything else divide over the thousand years, and have since the early centuries. Amillennialists read it as the present age between the cross and the return; postmillennialists as a coming era of gospel success; premillennialists as a literal reign after Christ returns. Each can point to real evidence. What all three hold is what the chapter is actually for: Christ reigns, his people are secure, and evil is finally and completely dealt with. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

21.t: Not escape from creation but its renewal. The dwelling of God is with man — the sentence Eden lost and the whole Bible has been moving back toward.
Because God and the Lamb are its temple. The whole sacrificial system ends by becoming unnecessary.

22.t: One voice claims to be the Alpha and Omega, the First and the Last, and four verses later identifies itself: I, Jesus, sent my angel. No change of speaker is marked between.
The Spirit and the bride say it, and then anyone who wishes may take the water of life freely. The Bible ends with an invitation.

8.t: Half an hour of it, before the trumpets. The prayers of the saints go up with the incense — they are part of what sets the sequence in motion.

9.t: Locusts and horsemen, drawing on Joel. The chapter ends noting that the survivors still did not repent, which is its actual point.

10.t: John eats it and finds it sweet then bitter, as Ezekiel did. Speaking God's word is both of those things.

11.t: Drawing on Moses, Elijah and Zechariah 4. Identifications vary widely; the pattern — testimony, apparent defeat, vindication — does not.
The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord. Handel set these words, and the tense is decisive: it is announced as already done.

14.t: A deliberate counterpoint to the beast of chapter 13. The 144,000 are marked on the forehead as the beast's followers are.
Proclaimed to every nation, tribe, language and people — even here, judgement and invitation run together.

15.h: The song of Moses and of the Lamb
15.t: Exodus imagery: those who have come through the sea stand beside it and sing. The last plagues follow.

16.t: The final sequence, echoing the plagues on Egypt. Verse 15 interrupts with a beatitude on the one who stays awake — the pastoral aim showing through the symbolism.

17.t: A city on seven hills, drunk on the blood of the saints, which first-century readers would have read as Rome. The name stands for every power that sets itself against God.

18.t: A dirge sung by kings, merchants and sailors, all of whom mourn the loss of trade rather than of people. Verse 13 ends the cargo list with human beings.

1.ctx: The book’s title is its first word in Greek, apokalypsis, ‘unveiling’. See History & setting of Revelation above.
1.mean: ‘This is the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to show His servants what must soon come to pass.’ It came through an angel to John, ‘who testifies to everything he saw.’ It is the first book of the Bible to promise a blessing on its readers: ‘Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear and obey what is written in it, because the time is near.’
1.big: Revelation is God’s unveiling of Jesus Christ, given to be read aloud in church and obeyed.

1.ctx: The seven churches lay on a circular road in the province of Asia, in the order a messenger would reach them. Seven is the number of completeness in Revelation, so they also stand for the whole church.
1.mean: ‘Grace and peace to you from Him who is and was and is to come, and from the seven spirits before His throne, and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth.’ Then praise: ‘To Him who loves us and has released us from our sins by His blood, who has made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God and Father’. ‘Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him—even those who pierced Him.’ ‘“I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God’.
1.big: Grace comes from Father, Spirit and Son; Jesus, who loves us and freed us by his blood, is coming visibly to rule.
1.diff: ‘The seven spirits’ (BSB footnote: ‘Or the sevenfold Spirit’) is usually understood as the Holy Spirit in his fullness (seven being the number of completeness; compare Isaiah 11:2 and Zechariah 4), since grace comes from them alongside the Father and Jesus. Some take them as seven chief angels. Alpha and Omega (the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet) is said here by ‘the Lord God’, and later by Jesus himself (22:13).

1.ctx: ‘The Lord’s day’ is one of the earliest uses of this name for Sunday, the day of the resurrection.
1.mean: John, ‘your brother and partner in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance’, was on Patmos ‘because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus.’ ‘On the Lord’s day I was in the Spirit’. He saw seven golden lampstands, ‘and among the lampstands was One like the Son of Man’: white hair, blazing eyes, a voice ‘like the roar of many waters’, a sword from his mouth, his face ‘like the sun shining at its brightest.’ John fell as though dead. ‘Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last, the Living One. I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever! And I hold the keys of Death and of Hades.’
1.big: The risen Christ walks among his churches, holds the keys of death, and tells his people not to be afraid.
1.diff: The figure John sees combines Daniel’s ‘one like a son of man’ (Daniel 7:13) with features Daniel gives to God himself, ‘the Ancient of Days’ (white hair, Daniel 7:9), and to a heavenly being (Daniel 10:5–6). ‘The First and the Last’ is God’s own title in Isaiah 44:6. Revelation repeatedly gives Jesus the titles of God.

b: Patmos is a small, rocky island in the Aegean Sea, about 55 km (35 miles) off the coast of what is now Turkey, roughly 12 km long. The phrase ‘because of the word of God and my testimony’ suggests John was there as a punishment, not as a missionary. Early tradition (Irenaeus, Eusebius, Jerome) says he was exiled there in the 14th year of Domitian (about AD 95) and released to return to Ephesus under the emperor Nerva in AD 96.

2.ctx: Each of the seven letters follows a pattern: a title of Christ from the vision of chapter 1, praise, criticism, a call to repent, and a promise ‘to the one who overcomes’.
2.mean: Christ praises the church’s hard work and endurance and its testing of false apostles. ‘But I have this against you: You have abandoned your first love. Therefore, keep in mind how far you have fallen. Repent and perform the deeds you did at first.’ Otherwise, ‘I will come to you and remove your lampstand’. They rightly hate ‘the works of the Nicolaitans’. ‘To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God.’
2.big: Sound doctrine and hard work are not enough if love has gone.
2.diff: ‘First love’ may mean love for Christ, love for one another, or both. A church can be orthodox, busy and loveless, and Christ counts that a fall.

b: Ephesus was the greatest city of the province of Asia, home of the famous temple of Artemis, and the centre of Paul’s longest ministry (Acts 19). By John’s time it also had its first temple to the emperors, built under Domitian, which made it a ‘temple warden’ of the imperial cult. Early tradition says John himself lived and died there. The ‘Nicolaitans’ cannot be identified with certainty; many think they taught that Christians could take part in pagan guild meals and their immorality (compare 2:14–15).

2.mean: ‘These are the words of the First and the Last, who died and returned to life. b: Smyrna (modern Izmir) was a rich and beautiful port, fiercely loyal to Rome. It was chosen over rival cities to build a temple to the emperor Tiberius (Tacitus, Annals 4.55–56), and statues and dedications to later emperors, Domitian among them, have been found there. Its bishop Polycarp, who had known John, was martyred there in the mid-2nd century. Asked to curse Christ, he answered: ‘Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?’ The account of his death says local Jews joined in the accusations, which may help explain the harsh words about ‘a synagogue of Satan’.

2.ctx: Balaam advised the Moabite king Balak to lure Israel into idolatry and immorality (Numbers 25; 31:16).
2.mean: ‘I know where you live, where the throne of Satan sits, yet you hold fast to My name.’ They did not deny the faith even when ‘My faithful witness Antipas’ was killed. But some ‘hold to the teaching of Balaam’, eating ‘food sacrificed to idols’ and committing ‘sexual immorality’, and some follow the Nicolaitans. ‘Therefore repent!’ ‘To the one who overcomes, I will give the hidden manna. 2.diff: The ‘white stone’ has many suggested backgrounds: a token of acquittal in a trial, a ticket of admission to a feast, or an amulet with a secret name. Whatever its exact background, it promises acceptance and a personal relationship with Christ.

hist.t: Pergamum: ‘where the throne of Satan sits’
b: Pergamum was built on a steep hill rising about 300 metres above the plain, crowded with temples: to Athena, Zeus, Dionysus, and Asclepius, the healing god whose symbol was a serpent. Its huge altar of Zeus, excavated by German archaeologists from 1878, now stands in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. It also had a temple honouring Rome and the deified Augustus, a focus of the imperial cult across the province, and it had been the seat of Roman government, where the governor had ‘the right of the sword’ (compare ‘the sharp, double-edged sword’, verse 12).

What is ‘the throne of Satan’? Suggestions include the great altar of Zeus, the cult of Asclepius, or, most likely in the view of many scholars, the imperial cult and Roman power, which had already cost Antipas his life.

2.ctx: Thyatira was a trade town known for its guilds, including dyers and wool-workers (Lydia, ‘a dealer in purple cloth’, came from there, Acts 16:14). Guild membership involved feasts in honour of pagan gods.
2.mean: Christ praises their growing love, faith, service and perseverance. ‘But I have this against you: You tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess.’ She teaches believers ‘to be sexually immoral and to eat food sacrificed to idols.’ She has had time to repent and refused; judgement will come, so ‘all the churches will know that I am the One who searches minds and hearts’. To the rest: ‘hold fast to what you have until I come.’
2.big: Christ searches hearts, and will not tolerate teaching that makes compromise with idolatry respectable.
2.diff: ‘Jezebel’ is probably a nickname, recalling Ahab’s queen who led Israel into Baal worship (1 Kings 16–21). The issue is not that a woman prophesied (compare Acts 21:9), but what she taught.

3.mean: ‘You have a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead. Wake up and strengthen what remains’. ‘If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know the hour’. A few ‘have not soiled their garments’; they ‘will walk with Me in white.’ ‘And I will never blot out his name from the Book of Life, but I will confess his name before My Father and His angels.’
3.big: A church can have a lively reputation and be spiritually dead; Christ calls it to wake up.
3.diff: ‘I will never blot out his name’ (verse 5) is a promise. Reformed readers take it as assurance that true believers will never be lost. Arminian readers take it to imply that a name could be removed from someone who does not overcome. Both take the promise as encouragement to persevere.

b: Sardis had been the capital of the wealthy kingdom of Lydia, with a citadel on a high, steep hill thought impossible to capture. Yet in 546 BC Cyrus of Persia took it by surprise, after a defender who dropped his helmet gave away a secret way up. It was captured again by Antiochus III in about 213 BC. ‘To capture the acropolis of Sardis’ became a saying for doing the impossible. Christ’s warning, ‘If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief’, would have stung. The church seems to have taken it to heart: in the 2nd century its bishop Melito was a respected Christian writer.

3.ctx: ‘The key of David’ echoes Isaiah 22:22, where authority over the royal palace is given to a faithful steward.
3.mean: ‘I have placed before you an open door, which no one can shut. I know that you have only a little strength, yet you have kept My word and have not denied My name.’ Their opponents will one day acknowledge ‘that I love you.’ ‘Because you have kept My command to persevere, I will also keep you from the hour of testing that is about to come upon the whole world’. ‘The one who overcomes I will make a pillar in the temple of My God, and he will never again leave it.’

3.diff: ‘Keep you from the hour of testing’ (verse 10). Dispensational futurists read this as a promise that the church will be removed from the earth (the ‘rapture’) before a future seven-year tribulation. Dallas Theological Seminary’s doctrinal statement, for example, teaches that ‘the translation of the church will be followed by the fulfillment of Israel’s seventieth week’. Most other interpreters (amillennial, postmillennial and historic premillennial) read it as a promise to protect believers through trial, not to remove them from it; Jesus uses the same Greek phrase, ‘keep… from’, when he prays not that the Father would take his disciples out of the world but keep them from the evil one (John 17:15). Wesley, in his day, read it as an exemption for that church: ‘O happy exemption from that spreading calamity!’

hist.t: Philadelphia and the earthquake of AD 17
b: Philadelphia was a smaller city on a major road east, in an earthquake zone. A great earthquake in AD 17 devastated it along with Sardis and other cities; the emperor Tiberius remitted their taxes for five years so they could rebuild (Tacitus, Annals 2.47). To a city that had been shaken apart, the promise ‘I will make a pillar in the temple of My God, and he will never again leave it’ would have meant a great deal.

3.ctx: The only church with nothing good said about it. See Laodicea: rich, lukewarm and blind below.
3.mean: ‘These are the words of the Amen, the faithful and true Witness, the Originator of God’s creation. I know your deeds; you are neither cold nor hot.’ ‘So because you are lukewarm—neither hot nor cold—I am about to vomit you out of My mouth!’ ‘You say, “I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing.” But you do not realize that you are wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked.’ Christ offers true gold, white clothes and eye salve. ‘Those I love I rebuke and discipline.’ ‘Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me.’
3.big: Self-satisfied religion is useless to Christ, yet he still knocks, offering everything they lack.
3.diff: ‘The Originator of God’s creation’ (BSB footnote: ‘Or Beginning or Ruler’). Jehovah’s Witnesses translate ‘the beginning of the creation by God’ and take it to mean Jesus was the first thing God created. The Greek word archē can mean beginning, origin or ruler; the historic reading is that Christ is the source and ruler of creation (compare John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). Wesley: ‘The Author, Prince, and Ruler’. ‘I stand at the door and knock’ is often used in evangelism, and rightly expresses Christ’s invitation; in context it is addressed to a church that has shut him out.

b: Laodicea was a wealthy banking centre, known for its textiles and wool and for a medical school famous for treating eyes. When an earthquake destroyed it in AD 60, it ‘recovered by its own resources’, refusing help from Rome (Tacitus, Annals 14.27). That background gives force to ‘I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing’, and to Christ’s offer of gold, ‘white garments’ and ‘salve to anoint your eyes’.

Many scholars link ‘neither cold nor hot’ to the city’s water, which came by aqueduct and arrived lukewarm, unlike the hot springs of nearby Hierapolis (useful for healing) and the cold water of Colossae (refreshing). On this reading the point is not ‘cold’ = hostile, ‘hot’ = keen, but that Laodicea was useful for nothing. Others (for example Craig Koester) question this background. The overall point is clear either way.

Most interpreters see it simply as John being taken up in the Spirit to receive the vision.

4.ctx: The scene draws on Ezekiel 1 and Isaiah 6.
4.mean: Lightning and thunder come from the throne; before it is ‘something like a sea of glass’. Four living creatures, like a lion, a calf, a man and an eagle, never stop saying: ‘Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!’ The elders cast their crowns before the throne, saying: ‘Worthy are You, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things; by Your will they exist and were created.’
4.big: All creation exists to worship its holy Creator.
4.diff: ‘Our Lord and God’ was exactly the title Domitian demanded (see Emperor worship in the province of Asia). Heaven gives it to the Creator alone. Christian tradition has linked the four living creatures with the four Gospels (since Irenaeus), but that is an application, not John’s meaning.

5.ctx: A scroll ‘sealed with seven seals’ was like a legal document or will, which only an authorised person could open. It contains God’s plan for judging and redeeming the world.
5.mean: No one is found worthy to open the scroll, and John weeps. ‘Do not weep! Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed to open the scroll’. John turns and sees not a lion but ‘a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne’. When he takes the scroll the creatures and elders fall down and sing a new song: ‘Worthy are You to take the scroll and open its seals, because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation.’
5.big: The Lion of Judah conquers as the slain Lamb: Christ’s victory is won through his sacrificial death.
5.diff: Lion and Lamb. John hears of a Lion and sees a Lamb. Many interpreters take this as the key to the whole book: the Messiah’s power is shown in his sacrifice. ‘Appeared to have been slain, standing’ holds together his death and resurrection. ‘Purchased for God’ people from every nation: the church is international by design.

5.ctx: The circle of worship widens from the throne to every creature.
5.mean: Countless angels sing: ‘Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!’ Then every creature everywhere: ‘To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever!’ ‘And the four living creatures said, “Amen,” and the elders fell down and worshiped.’
5.big: The Lamb receives the same worship as God on the throne.
5.diff: Revelation twice forbids worshipping an angel (19:10; 22:8–9): ‘Worship God!’ Yet here the Lamb receives the very worship given to God. This is one of the clearest pointers in the New Testament to Jesus’ full deity.

6.h: The First Seal: The White Horse
6.ctx: The first four seals bring four horsemen, echoing Zechariah 1:8–11 and 6:1–8.
6.mean: As the Lamb opens the first seal: ‘I looked and saw a white horse, and its rider held a bow. And he was given a crown, and he rode out to overcome and conquer.’
6.big: Conquest and war are let loose, but only when the Lamb opens the seal.
6.diff: Who is the rider? Some identify him with Christ, who rides a white horse in 19:11, so the first seal is the gospel going out conquering. Many others, noting that the other three riders bring disaster, take him as a false conqueror or military conquest. The Parthians to Rome’s east were famous mounted archers, and some think readers would have thought of them. All the horsemen are under the Lamb’s control: they go out when he opens the seals.

6.ctx: The second of the four horsemen.
6.mean: ‘Then another horse went forth. It was bright red, and its rider was granted permission to take away peace from the earth and to make men slay one another. And he was given a great sword.’
6.big: Bloodshed comes only by permission; it is not outside God’s rule.

6.ctx: A denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer (BSB footnote).
6.mean: ‘I looked and saw a black horse, and its rider held in his hand a pair of scales.’ A voice says: ‘A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the oil and wine.’
6.big: Famine prices strike the poor while luxuries are spared.
6.diff: A day’s wage for one person’s daily food is a famine price, many times normal. Sparing ‘the oil and wine’ suggests the hardship falls on basic food, and so on the poor, while the comfortable carry on.

6.ctx: The last of the four horsemen.
6.mean: ‘I looked and saw a pale green horse. Its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed close behind. And they were given authority over a fourth of the earth, to kill by sword, by famine, by plague, and by the beasts of the earth.’
6.big: Death has limited authority: a fourth, not all.
6.diff: Judgements in Revelation grow in stages (a fourth here, a third in the trumpets, then all in the bowls). The limits show both God’s control and his patience, leaving time to repent (9:20–21).

6.ctx: In the temple, the blood of sacrifices was poured out at the base of the altar.
6.mean: ‘I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony they had upheld.’ ‘How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You judge those who dwell upon the earth and avenge our blood?’ ‘Then each of them was given a white robe and told to rest a little while longer’ until the number of martyrs is complete.
6.big: God hears the cry of his suffering people, and justice, though delayed, will come.
6.diff: The cry ‘how long’ echoes the psalms of lament (Psalm 13; 79:5–10). Asking God for justice is not the same as personal revenge; it leaves vengeance to God (Romans 12:19). The passage also shows those who have died for Christ as alive and conscious with God, awaiting the end.

6.ctx: Earthquakes were well known in this region (see Philadelphia and Laodicea).
6.mean: ‘There was a great earthquake, and the sun became black like sackcloth of goat hair, and the whole moon turned blood red, and the stars of the sky fell to the earth’. Kings, generals, the rich, slave and free hide in caves: ‘Fall on us and hide us from the face of the One seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb. For the great day of Their wrath has come, and who is able to withstand it?’
6.big: On the day of God’s wrath, no rank or wealth will protect anyone.
6.diff: This language of a shaken universe comes from the prophets (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4; Joel 2:31), where it often pictures the fall of empires. Interpreters differ on whether it describes the final day or great judgements in history. ‘The wrath of the Lamb’ is a striking phrase: the Lamb is gentle, but not harmless.

7.ctx: A pause before the seventh seal. In Ezekiel 9:4 a mark was placed on the foreheads of the faithful to protect them from judgement.
7.mean: Four angels hold back the winds of judgement ‘until we have placed a seal on the foreheads of the servants of our God.’ ‘And I heard the number of those who were sealed, 144,000 from all the tribes of Israel’: 12,000 from each of twelve tribes.
7.big: Before judgement falls, God marks and protects his own.
7.diff: Who are the 144,000? Most interpreters take the number as symbolic of the whole people of God (12 x 12 x 1,000: complete), the same company John then sees as ‘a multitude too large to count’ (verse 9). He hears a number and sees a multitude, as he heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb (5:5–6). The list of tribes is unusual (Dan is missing, Joseph and Manasseh are both included), which also suggests a symbolic list. Dispensational futurists take the 144,000 as Jewish believers in a future tribulation. Jehovah’s Witnesses teach that ‘only 144,000 tried and faithful persons will be taken there to rule with Christ’, while others live on earth. Most Christians reject this, since the New Testament promises all believers a place with Christ (John 14:2–3; Philippians 1:23).

src.l: Watch Tower Society, You Can Live Forever in Paradise on Earth, ‘Who Go to Heaven, and Why?’

7.ctx: Palm branches were waved at the Feast of Tabernacles and at victory celebrations (compare John 12:13).
7.mean: ‘I looked and saw a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb.’ ‘Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!’ ‘These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.’ ‘For the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd. “He will lead them to springs of living water,” and “God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”’
7.big: A countless, worldwide multitude, washed by the Lamb’s blood, will be shepherded by him for ever.
7.diff: ‘The great tribulation’ is read by futurists as a specific future period, and by others as the whole experience of suffering faithful believers in this age (compare 1:9, where John is already their ‘partner in the tribulation’).

8.ctx: In the temple, incense was offered at the golden altar while the people prayed (Luke 1:9–10).
8.mean: ‘When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.’ Seven angels are given seven trumpets. Another angel offers incense ‘along with the prayers of all the saints’. ‘And the smoke of the incense, together with the prayers of the saints, rose up before God’. Then the angel fills the censer with fire from the altar and hurls it to the earth: thunder, lightning and an earthquake.
8.big: The prayers of God’s people rise before him and play a part in his action in the world.
8.diff: Structure. Many interpreters think the seals, trumpets and bowls do not follow one another in strict order, but cover the same ground from different angles, each ending at the final judgement (a pattern called ‘recapitulation’). Futurists more often read them as a sequence of future events.

8.ctx: Trumpets announced battle, festivals and the presence of God (Joshua 6; Exodus 19:16). These judgements echo the plagues of Egypt.
8.mean: Hail and fire burn a third of the earth; something like a burning mountain turns a third of the sea to blood; a star called ‘Wormwood’ makes a third of the waters bitter; a third of the sun, moon and stars are darkened. An eagle cries: ‘Woe! Woe! Woe to those who dwell on the earth’.
8.big: God’s judgements, like the plagues of Egypt, warn a rebellious world, but are still limited.
8.diff: Some read these as literal future catastrophes, some as symbols of disasters throughout history, some as specific historical events. All agree they echo Exodus: God judges the oppressors of his people as he did Pharaoh, and the limit (‘a third’) leaves room to repent.

9.ctx: The imagery draws on the locust plague of Joel 1–2, where locusts are pictured as an invading army.
9.mean: A fallen star is given the key to ‘the pit of the Abyss’. Out of the smoke come locusts with power to torment, ‘but only those who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads.’ ‘In those days men will seek death and will not find it’. Their king is ‘the angel of the Abyss. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek it is Apollyon’, both meaning Destroyer.
9.big: Demonic forces torment those without God’s seal, but God’s people are protected.
9.diff: Readings vary widely: demonic powers, invading armies, or the self-destruction of sin. What is clear is that the forces of evil are given limited permission, and God’s sealed people are not their target.

9.ctx: The Euphrates was Rome’s eastern frontier, beyond which lay the Parthian empire, feared for its cavalry.
9.mean: Four angels bound at the Euphrates are released ‘to kill a third of mankind’, with mounted troops numbering ‘two hundred million’. Yet ‘the rest of mankind who were not killed by these plagues still did not repent of the works of their hands’. They went on worshipping demons and idols, and did not repent ‘of their murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, and theft.’
9.big: Judgement alone does not change hearts; people can see disaster and still refuse to repent.

10.h: The Angel and the Small Scroll
10.ctx: Ezekiel too was given a scroll to eat (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3).
10.mean: A mighty angel stands on sea and land, and swears: ‘There will be no more delay!’ At the seventh trumpet ‘the mystery of God will be fulfilled’. John is told to eat a small scroll: ‘It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be as sweet as honey.’ ‘You must prophesy again about many peoples and nations and tongues and kings.’
10.big: God’s word is sweet to receive and bitter to carry, and his prophet must take it in before passing it on.
10.diff: That John may not write down what the seven thunders said (verse 4) is a reminder that Revelation does not tell us everything about the future.

11.ctx: 42 months, 1,260 days and ‘a time, and times, and half a time’ (12:14) all equal three and a half years, a period from Daniel (7:25; 12:7) for a limited time of persecution.
11.mean: John is told to measure the temple, but not the outer court, which is given to the nations to trample for 42 months. God’s ‘two witnesses’ prophesy for 1,260 days in sackcloth. They are ‘the two olive trees and the two lampstands’ (compare Zechariah 4). Like Elijah they can shut the sky; like Moses they can turn water to blood.
11.big: God protects his people’s witness through a limited time of opposition.
11.diff: The two witnesses have been identified as Moses and Elijah returning, as two future individuals, or (since they are called ‘lampstands’, the symbol for churches in 1:20) as the witnessing church. The temple. Some who date Revelation before AD 70 take this as the Jerusalem temple, still standing. Others note that John often uses ‘temple’ for God’s people (3:12) and read it symbolically.

src.l: ‘Revelation, Book of’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

11.ctx: ‘The beast’ appears here for the first time; it is described in chapter 13.
11.mean: When their testimony is finished, the beast kills them. Their bodies lie in ‘the great city—figuratively called Sodom and Egypt—where their Lord was also crucified.’ The world celebrates. ‘But after the three and a half days, the breath of life from God entered the two witnesses, and they stood on their feet’, and they go up to heaven in a cloud as their enemies watch. In the earthquake that follows, ‘the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.’
11.big: Faithful witnesses may be silenced for a time, but God raises and vindicates them, as he did their Lord.

11.ctx: The final trumpet brings the story to its end, before chapter 12 goes back to tell it again from another angle.
11.mean: ‘The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever.’ The elders give thanks: ‘You have taken Your great power and have begun to reign.’ It is time ‘to judge the dead and to reward Your servants’, ‘and to destroy those who destroy the earth.’ ‘Then the temple of God in heaven was opened, and the ark of His covenant appeared’.
11.big: The end of history is the open, eternal reign of God and his Christ.
11.diff: Handel set verse 15 in the Hallelujah Chorus of Messiah. The verbs speak of the outcome as already done: from heaven’s point of view, it is certain.

12.ctx: A new section begins, going behind the scenes of history. The dragon is identified in verse 9 as Satan.
12.mean: ‘A woman clothed in the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head’ is in labour. A ‘huge red dragon with seven heads, ten horns’ waits to devour her child. ‘And she gave birth to a son, a male child, who will rule all the nations with an iron scepter. And her child was caught up to God and to His throne.’ The woman flees into the wilderness, where God cares for her.
12.big: Satan tried to destroy the Messiah and failed; now God protects his people.
12.diff: Who is the woman? Most interpreters understand her as the people of God: Israel, from whom the Messiah came (the twelve stars recall the twelve tribes, Genesis 37:9), and then the church, persecuted after his ascension. Catholic and Orthodox tradition has also seen in her Mary, the mother of the Messiah, while generally agreeing she stands for God’s people too. The child is clearly Christ (Psalm 2:9), born, then ‘caught up to God’: his whole life, death and resurrection summed up in one line.

12.ctx: Michael is the angel who protects God’s people in Daniel 10:13 and 12:1.
12.mean: ‘Michael and his angels fought against the dragon’, and the dragon was thrown down: ‘that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world.’ A voice in heaven: ‘For the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down’. ‘They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony. And they did not love their lives so as to shy away from death.’ The devil is furious, ‘knowing he has only a short time.’
12.big: Satan is defeated by the Lamb’s blood, and believers overcome him by faithful witness.
12.diff: Many interpreters connect Satan’s being thrown down with Christ’s death and exaltation (compare John 12:31: ‘now the prince of this world will be cast out’). Others see a primeval fall of Satan, or a future event. The victory hymn (verses 10–12) ties it to ‘the blood of the Lamb’.

12.ctx: The eagle’s wings recall Exodus 19:4: ‘I carried you on eagles’ wings’.
12.mean: Thrown down, the dragon pursues the woman, ‘But the woman was given two wings of a great eagle to fly’ to the wilderness, where she is cared for ‘for a time, and times, and half a time.’ The earth swallows the flood the serpent sends. ‘And the dragon was enraged at the woman and went to make war with the rest of her children, who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus.’
12.big: A defeated but furious enemy attacks God’s people, but God sustains them.

13.ctx: The beast combines the four beasts of Daniel 7 (leopard, bear, lion, ten horns), Daniel’s picture of world empires that oppose God.
13.mean: A beast rises out of the sea with ten horns and seven heads, ‘and the dragon gave the beast his power and his throne and great authority.’ One head seemed mortally wounded, ‘But the mortal wound was healed, and the whole world marveled and followed the beast.’ ‘Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?’ It blasphemes for 42 months and is ‘permitted to wage war against the saints and to conquer them’. All worship it except those whose names are in ‘the Book of Life belonging to the Lamb who was slain.’ ‘Here is a call for the perseverance and faith of the saints.’
13.big: Satan works through political power that demands worship, and believers must endure faithfully.
13.diff: Who is the beast? Preterists and most scholars: the Roman empire and its emperors, demanding worship; the healed wound may echo the belief that Nero would return (see the note on 13:16). Historicists, including most Reformers and Wesley, took it as the papacy; Wesley: ‘This beast is the Romish Papacy’. Most Protestants today do not hold this. Futurists: a future world ruler, the Antichrist. Idealists: every state power that sets itself up as God and persecutes his people. These are not exclusive; many see Rome as the first fulfilment of a pattern that recurs and will climax before Christ returns. See the glossary entry ‘Antichrist’.

src.l: John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Revelation 13
‘Revelation, Book of’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

13.mean: ‘Another beast rising out of the earth. This beast had two horns like a lamb, but spoke like a dragon.’ It makes people worship the first beast, performs ‘great signs, even causing fire from heaven to come down’, and has an image of the beast made, which can speak and have those who refuse to worship it killed.
13.big: False religion, looking gentle but speaking for Satan, persuades people to worship power.
13.diff: In John’s setting this fits the local priests and officials of the imperial cult in Asia, who promoted emperor worship and could enforce it. In every age it stands for religion that serves the powers of the world rather than God.

src.l: ‘Ephesus’, ‘Smyrna’, ‘Pergamum’, ‘Thyatira’, ‘Sardis’, ‘Philadelphia’ and ‘Laodicea’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Hemer, Ramsay, Yamauchi, Kraybill)

13.ctx: Slaves and soldiers could be marked or branded to show whom they belonged to. Contrast the seal of God on his people’s foreheads (7:3).
13.mean: The second beast requires everyone ‘to receive a mark on their right hand or on their forehead, so that no one could buy or sell unless he had the mark—the name of the beast or the number of its name. Here is a call for wisdom: Let the one who has insight calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and that number is 666.’
13.big: The world demands a visible loyalty that can cost believers their livelihood; God’s people belong to him.
13.diff: What is the mark? Scholars have suggested several backgrounds: the brands or tattoos given to slaves, captured soldiers or devotees of a god; imperial seals on documents of sale; or the emperor’s image on coins. None fits exactly. Since God’s seal on his people (7:3; 14:1) is not a visible tattoo, most interpreters take the beast’s mark the same way: belonging and loyalty shown in thinking (forehead) and action (hand). In John’s world, refusing the imperial cult and guild sacrifices could shut a believer out of trade. Some futurists expect a literal mark, and over the years it has been linked to tattoos, barcodes, microchips and vaccines; such speculation has repeatedly proved wrong and has caused needless fear. 666: see the drop-down below.

hist.t: 666, Nero, and ‘the number of a man’
b: In the ancient world, letters doubled as numbers, so any name could be added up to a total. John invites readers to ‘calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man’.

The most widely held explanation is that 666 is the total of ‘Nero Caesar’ written in Hebrew letters; many modern scholars read the beast against the background of Roman imperial religion and the figure of Nero. Some ancient manuscripts read 616 (BSB footnote), including the oldest surviving copy of this verse, a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt (P115, 3rd or early 4th century). Irenaeus knew of this variant and thought it a copyist’s error. Supporters of the Nero view point out that 616 is exactly what the name gives if spelled without its final ‘n’ (Nero rather than Neron, the Latin form), which would explain why both numbers circulated; the textual scholar P. J. Williams accepts that 616 can be explained this way, though he cautions against treating it as proof and suggests it may also have been chosen because it looked like abbreviations for Jesus’ name. There was also a widespread belief that Nero would return: Suetonius says that after his death some set up statues and published edicts of his, ‘as if he were still alive and would shortly return and deal destruction to his enemies’, and that ‘twenty years later’ a pretender claiming to be Nero was supported by the Parthians. Many see this behind the beast’s ‘mortal wound’ that was healed (13:3).

Objections. The New Bible Dictionary notes that it is hard to see why a Greek book would use a Hebrew spelling, and that a less usual spelling is needed to reach 666. Irenaeus himself, about AD 180, did not know of the Nero solution, and warned against confidently naming the Antichrist. Others take 666 symbolically: six falls short of seven, the number of perfection, three times over, so it is the number of humanity trying to be God and always falling short. Historicist interpreters, including Wesley, applied it to the papacy; countless other names have been proposed through history, which is a warning against confident calculation.

14.ctx: Mount Zion is the hill of Jerusalem where God dwelt with his people, set against the beast’s domain.
14.mean: ‘I looked and saw the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with Him 144,000 who had His name and His Father’s name written on their foreheads.’ They sing a new song that only they can learn. ‘These are the ones who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins. They follow the Lamb wherever He goes.’ They are ‘firstfruits to God and to the Lamb’, and ‘no lie was found in their mouths’.
14.big: Those who belong to the Lamb follow him wherever he goes, pure and truthful.
14.diff: ‘Not been defiled with women’ is generally understood as a picture of spiritual faithfulness, since idolatry is often called adultery in the Old Testament; it does not mean sex in marriage defiles (Hebrews 13:4). Israel’s soldiers kept themselves from sexual relations before battle (1 Samuel 21:5), and some see that background here: the 144,000 are God’s army. See the note on 7:1 for who they are.

14.h: The Three Angels and Babylon’s Fall
14.ctx: ‘Babylon’, the empire that destroyed Jerusalem, is John’s name for the great city opposed to God (described in chapters 17–18).
14.mean: An angel proclaims ‘the eternal gospel’ to every nation: ‘Fear God and give Him glory, because the hour of His judgment has come.’ A second: ‘Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great’. A third warns that anyone who worships the beast ‘will drink the wine of God’s anger’ and ‘the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever.’ ‘Here is a call for the perseverance of the saints’. ‘Blessed are the dead—those who die in the Lord from this moment on.’ ‘They will rest from their labors, for their deeds will follow them.’
14.big: God’s final call goes out to all nations; the choice between God and the beast has eternal consequences.
14.diff: Eternal punishment. The historic teaching of the churches is that the wicked ‘shall be cast into eternal torments, and be punished with everlasting destruction’ (Westminster Confession 33.2). Some evangelicals hold ‘conditional immortality’ (annihilationism): the wicked are finally destroyed rather than punished for ever, and ‘the smoke… rises forever’ describes a final, lasting destruction. Seventh-day Adventists teach that ‘fire from God will consume them and cleanse the earth’. Most Christians have held the traditional view, citing passages such as Matthew 25:46 and Revelation 20:10. The three angels. Seventh-day Adventists see their own mission in these verses: their proclamation ‘is symbolized by the three angels of Revelation 14’.

14.ctx: Joel 3:13: ‘Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe’; and Isaiah 63:1–6, the Lord treading the winepress of judgement.
14.mean: ‘One like the Son of Man’ on a white cloud swings his sickle, ‘and the earth was harvested.’ Then an angel gathers ‘the grapes of the earth’ and throws them ‘into the great winepress of God’s wrath’, and blood flows ‘as high as the bridles of the horses for a distance of 1,600 stadia’ (about 184 miles, or 296 km).
14.big: History ends in a harvest: the gathering of God’s people and the judgement of the wicked.
14.diff: The two harvests are read by many as the gathering of the saved (grain, by the Son of Man) and the judgement of the wicked (grapes). Others see both as judgement. 1,600 (40 x 40, or 4 x 4 x 100) is probably symbolic of a complete, worldwide judgement.

15.h: The Song of Moses and the Lamb
15.ctx: After crossing the Red Sea, Moses and Israel sang a song of victory (Exodus 15).
15.mean: John sees ‘seven angels with the seven final plagues, with which the wrath of God is completed.’ Beside ‘a sea of glass mixed with fire’ stand ‘those who had conquered the beast’, singing ‘the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb: “Great and wonderful are Your works, O Lord God Almighty! Just and true are Your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name? For You alone are holy. All nations will come and worship before You”’.
15.big: God’s people sing of a new exodus: deliverance through the Lamb and the coming worship of all nations.
15.diff: The song of the conquerors is entirely about God, not about themselves. It looks forward to ‘All nations’ worshipping him: even in a book full of judgement, the hope is for the nations to turn to God.

15.ctx: ‘The tabernacle of the Testimony’ was the tent in the wilderness where the tablets of the law were kept (Exodus 38:21).
15.mean: ‘The temple—the tabernacle of the Testimony—was opened in heaven.’ Seven angels come out, and are given ‘seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God’. ‘And the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from His power; and no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.’
15.big: God’s final judgements come from his holy presence, according to his law.

16.h: The First Six Bowls of Wrath
16.ctx: The bowls echo the plagues of Egypt (sores, water turned to blood, darkness, frogs), but now nothing is held back: no more ‘a third’.
16.mean: Sores, seas and rivers turned to blood, scorching heat, darkness on ‘the throne of the beast’. The angel of the waters declares God just: ‘they have spilled the blood of saints and prophets, and You have given them blood to drink’. Yet the people ‘cursed the name of God… Yet they did not repent and give Him glory.’ The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates, and demonic spirits gather the kings of the earth ‘for battle on the great day of God the Almighty’, ‘in the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.’ In the middle, Christ speaks: ‘Behold, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who remains awake’.
16.big: God’s judgements are just, yet hardened hearts curse him rather than repent.
16.diff: Armageddon. Futurists, especially dispensationalists, expect a literal final battle in the region of Megiddo in northern Israel. Many others read it as a symbol of the final gathering of the world’s powers against God, wherever and however that happens. See the drop-down below. The call to stay awake (verse 15) is the practical point: be ready.

b: ‘Armageddon’ (Greek Harmagedon) is a Hebrew name, most probably har Megiddo, ‘the mountain of Megiddo’. Megiddo was a fortified city guarding the main pass through the Carmel ridge on the great road between Egypt and Mesopotamia, and many battles were fought nearby: Deborah and Barak against the Canaanites (Judges 5:19), and Pharaoh Neco’s defeat of King Josiah (2 Kings 23:29).

Megiddo stood on a hill beside a plain, not on a mountain, and many who accept the identification take the name as symbolic: the place where the powers of the world gather against God, as so often against his people. Other scholars propose different Hebrew originals, such as ‘mount of assembly’. Notice that in Revelation the ‘battle’ is never described: the enemies are simply defeated (19:19–21; 20:9).

16.ctx: ‘It is done!’ echoes Jesus’ cry on the cross, ‘It is finished’ (John 19:30).
16.mean: ‘A loud voice came from the throne in the temple, saying, “It is done!”’ The greatest earthquake ever: ‘The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations collapsed. And God remembered Babylon the great’. Islands and mountains vanish; enormous hailstones fall. ‘And men cursed God’.
16.big: God’s judgement on the world’s proud city is complete.

17.ctx: In the prophets, cities that led others into idolatry and exploitation are pictured as prostitutes (Isaiah 23:15–17 of Tyre; Nahum 3:4 of Nineveh).
17.mean: An angel shows John ‘the great prostitute, who sits on many waters. The kings of the earth were immoral with her’. She sits on ‘a scarlet beast’ with seven heads and ten horns, dressed in purple and scarlet, with gold, jewels and pearls, holding ‘a golden cup full of abominations’. On her forehead: ‘BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.’
17.big: Worldly power and wealth that seduce people from God are pictured as a glamorous prostitute riding on the beast.
17.diff: Who is Babylon? Most interpreters: for John’s first readers, Rome; and in every age, the seductive world-system of power, wealth and idolatry opposed to God. Some preterists identify her with unfaithful Jerusalem. Historicist Protestants (including many Reformers) identified her with papal Rome; few Protestants hold this today. Some futurists expect a literal rebuilt Babylon or a future world city.

17.ctx: See Seven hills and seven kings below.
17.mean: ‘The woman was drunk with the blood of the saints and witnesses for Jesus.’ The angel explains: ‘The beast that you saw—it was, and now is no more, but is about to come up out of the Abyss and go to its destruction.’ ‘The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits. There are also seven kings. Five have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come.’ The beast ‘is an eighth king’. Ten kings will give their power to the beast for ‘one hour’.
17.big: The powers that persecute God’s people are temporary and heading for destruction.
17.diff: ‘This calls for a mind with wisdom’ (verse 9): John signals that the details are a puzzle meant for his first readers to recognise. Interpreters still debate how to count the kings; the message, that the beast’s time is short, is clear.

b: Rome was famous in the ancient world as the city on seven hills. Most scholars therefore agree that John’s first readers would have recognised ‘Babylon’ as Rome, ‘the great city that rules over the kings of the earth’ (17:18), as 1 Peter 5:13 also uses ‘Babylon’ for Rome.

The ‘seven kings’ (17:10) are harder. If they are emperors, it is unclear where to start counting (Julius Caesar or Augustus) and whether to include the three short-lived emperors of AD 68–69. Different counts give different dates for the book, which is why this verse features in the debate over when it was written. Many interpreters think seven is symbolic here, as everywhere in Revelation: a complete line of world rulers, with the end not far off. ‘The beast that was, and now is not’, an ‘eighth king’ belonging to the seven, may draw on the belief that Nero would return.

17.ctx: ‘Lord of lords and King of kings’ was a title used of God (Deuteronomy 10:17); ‘king of kings’ was also claimed by great eastern emperors (Daniel 2:37).
17.mean: ‘They will make war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will triumph over them, because He is Lord of lords and King of kings; and He will be accompanied by His called and chosen and faithful ones.’ In the end the beast and its allies turn on the prostitute and destroy her: ‘For God has put it into their hearts to carry out His purpose’. ‘The woman you saw is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth.’
17.big: Evil destroys itself, and the Lamb triumphs with his faithful people.
17.diff: Even the evil powers’ attack on Babylon serves God’s purpose (verse 17). Evil is not a rival god; it is under his control and turns on itself.

18.ctx: This chapter echoes the prophets’ laments over Babylon (Isaiah 21:9; Jeremiah 50–51) and Tyre (Ezekiel 26–27).
18.mean: ‘Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!’ Nations, kings and merchants have shared in her immorality and luxury. ‘Come out of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins or contract any of her plagues.’ She said in her heart, ‘I sit as queen; I am not a widow and will never see grief.’ ‘Therefore her plagues will come in one day’.
18.big: God’s people must come out of the world’s proud, luxurious system before it falls.
18.diff: ‘Come out of her’ is not a call to leave the physical city, but to refuse to share in its idolatry, injustice and love of luxury. Christians live in ‘Babylon’ but must not belong to it.

18.ctx: Rome imported luxury goods from across its empire and beyond. The list moves from gold and jewels down to animals, and finally to people.
18.mean: Kings, merchants and sailors stand far off and mourn, not for the city but for their lost profits: ‘Woe, woe to the great city… For in a single hour your judgment has come.’ The merchants list their cargo: gold, silver, jewels, silk, ivory, spices, wine, wheat, horses, carriages, and finally ‘bodies and souls of slaves.’ ‘For in a single hour such fabulous wealth has been destroyed!’ ‘Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets’.
18.big: An economy that treats people as cargo stands under God’s judgement.
18.diff: The list ends with ‘bodies and souls of slaves’, placing human beings at the bottom of a list of goods. Revelation exposes an economic system built on luxury and exploitation. Christians today ask what this means for how they earn, buy and invest.

18.ctx: Jeremiah told a messenger to tie a stone to his scroll against Babylon and throw it into the Euphrates (Jeremiah 51:63–64).
18.mean: ‘A mighty angel picked up a stone the size of a great millstone and cast it into the sea, saying: “With such violence the great city of Babylon will be cast down, never to be seen again.”’ No more music, trade, millstones, lamps, or wedding voices. ‘And there was found in her the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who had been slain on the earth.’
18.big: The proud city falls for ever, held to account for the blood of the innocent.

19.ctx: ‘Hallelujah’ is Hebrew for ‘Praise the LORD’ (BSB footnote).
19.mean: ‘Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God! For His judgments are true and just. He has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth’. ‘He has avenged the blood of His servants’. The elders and creatures worship: ‘Amen, Hallelujah!’
19.big: Heaven praises God because his judgements are true and just.
19.diff: ‘Hallelujah’ appears four times here (verses 1, 3, 4, 6) and nowhere else in the New Testament. Heaven rejoices not in suffering but in justice finally done for the oppressed.

19.ctx: The Old Testament pictures God as Israel’s husband (Hosea 2; Isaiah 54:5), and Jesus spoke of himself as the bridegroom (Mark 2:19).
19.mean: ‘Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Let us rejoice and be glad and give Him the glory. For the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready.’ Her fine linen ‘is the righteous acts of the saints.’ ‘Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.’ John falls to worship the angel, who says: ‘Do not do that! I am a fellow servant… Worship God!’
19.big: History ends in a wedding: Christ and his people united in joy for ever.
19.diff: Worship God alone. The angel’s refusal (again at 22:9) contrasts sharply with the worship freely given to the Lamb (5:8–14). The bride’s clothing is both ‘given’ to her and made of the saints’ righteous acts: grace and the fruit of grace together.

19.h: The Rider on the White Horse
19.ctx: This is Christ’s return, pictured as a victorious king.
19.mean: ‘I saw heaven standing open, and there before me was a white horse. And its rider is called Faithful and True. With righteousness He judges and wages war.’ He has many crowns and a secret name. ‘He is dressed in a robe dipped in blood, and His name is The Word of God.’ Heaven’s armies follow him. ‘From His mouth proceeds a sharp sword’. On his robe and thigh: ‘KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS.’
19.big: Christ will return as the faithful, true and righteous King, and every enemy will fall.
19.diff: His robe is ‘dipped in blood’ before any battle begins, which many take as his own blood: he conquers as the slain Lamb. His weapon is ‘a sharp sword’ from his mouth, his word. ‘The Word of God’ links this vision with John 1:1.

19.h: Defeat of the Beast and False Prophet
19.ctx: The grim ‘supper’ echoes Ezekiel 39:17–20, and contrasts with the marriage supper of the Lamb.
19.mean: An angel summons the birds to ‘the great supper of God’. ‘I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies assembled to wage war against the One seated on the horse’. ‘But the beast was captured along with the false prophet’. ‘Both the beast and the false prophet were thrown alive into the fiery lake of burning sulfur.’ The rest are killed ‘with the sword that proceeded from the mouth of the One seated on the horse.’
19.big: The great final battle is no contest: Christ’s word defeats every enemy.
19.diff: Revelation describes the gathering for battle (16:14; 19:19) but never a battle. The enemies are simply captured and destroyed by Christ’s word.

20.ctx: The only passage in the Bible to mention a thousand-year reign. See the glossary entry ‘Millennium’.
20.mean: An angel seizes ‘the dragon, that ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years’, ‘so that he could not deceive the nations until the thousand years were complete.’ John sees the souls of those beheaded for their testimony, who had not worshipped the beast: ‘they came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.’ ‘This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy are those who share in the first resurrection! The second death has no power over them’.
20.big: Satan’s power is limited, and those faithful to Christ, even to death, reign with him.
20.diff: The millennium. Premillennialists read this as a future thousand-year reign of Christ on earth after his return. It was the view of several early writers (Papias, Justin, Irenaeus), and today of many evangelicals; dispensationalists add a pre-tribulation rapture and a restored national Israel (Dallas Theological Seminary: ‘He will thus introduce the millennial age; bind Satan and place him in the abyss’). Amillennialists read the thousand years as a symbol of the present age: Satan was bound by Christ’s victory (Matthew 12:29) so that he cannot stop the gospel reaching the nations, and believers who have died reign with Christ in heaven (the ‘first resurrection’). Augustine taught that ‘the Church even now is the kingdom of Christ’; Aquinas, Luther and Calvin followed this line, and it is widely held in Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed churches. Postmillennialists expect a long golden age of gospel success before Christ returns; many Puritans held this. The Catholic Church ‘has rejected even modified forms of this falsification of the kingdom to come under the name of millenarianism’ (Catechism 676). All agree that Christ will return personally, raise the dead and judge, and that Satan is a defeated foe.

20.h: Satan Cast into the Lake of Fire
20.ctx: ‘Gog and Magog’ come from Ezekiel 38–39, the last great attack on God’s people.
20.mean: ‘When the thousand years are complete, Satan will be released from his prison, and will go out to deceive the nations’. They surround ‘the camp of the saints and the beloved city. But fire came down from heaven and consumed them. And the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur’. ‘There they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.’
20.big: Satan’s final rebellion fails instantly, and he is destroyed for ever.
20.diff: Many amillennial interpreters see this as the same final conflict as 16:14 and 19:19, told again from another angle. Premillennialists see a rebellion at the end of Christ’s earthly reign.

20.h: Judgment before the Great White Throne
20.ctx: The last judgement, of all the dead.
20.mean: ‘Then I saw a great white throne and the One seated on it. Earth and heaven fled from His presence’. ‘And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne. And books were opened, and one of them was the Book of Life. And the dead were judged according to their deeds’. ‘Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death’. ‘And if anyone was found whose name was not written in the Book of Life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.’
20.big: Everyone will stand before God, and only those written in the Lamb’s Book of Life are safe.
20.diff: Judged by deeds, saved by grace. Everyone is judged ‘according to their deeds’, yet what finally decides is whether a name is in ‘the Book of Life’, which is ‘the Lamb’s’ (21:27). Most Christians understand this as salvation by grace through Christ, shown in a changed life (compare Romans 2:6–7 with 3:23–24). The Westminster Confession says God has appointed this day so that people ‘may shake off all carnal security, and be always watchful’ (33.3). The second death and the lake of fire: see the note on 14:6 for views on eternal punishment. ‘Death and Hades’ themselves are destroyed: death will be no more.

21.h: A New Heaven and a New Earth
21.ctx: Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 promised ‘new heavens and a new earth’. For John’s readers the sea was a symbol of chaos and danger, and the source of the beast (13:1).
21.mean: ‘Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.’ ‘Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them.’ ‘“He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,” and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain’. ‘Behold, I make all things new.’ ‘To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life.’
21.big: The end is not escape from the world but a renewed creation where God lives with his people and every tear is wiped away.
21.diff: The city comes down from heaven to earth: the Christian hope is a renewed creation and the resurrection of the body, not souls floating in the sky. Christians differ on whether the present creation will be renewed or replaced, but most see continuity, as with the resurrection body (1 Corinthians 15). Verse 8 warns that the cowardly, unbelieving and unrepentant have no place there.

21.ctx: Ezekiel 40–48 also has a measured city with twelve gates. 12,000 stadia is about 1,380 miles or 2,220 km (BSB footnote).
21.mean: ‘Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.’ John sees the holy city, ‘shining with the glory of God’. Twelve gates bear ‘the names of the twelve tribes of Israel’; twelve foundations bear ‘the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.’ It is a perfect cube, ‘12,000 stadia in length and width and height’, built of gold and precious stones, its gates pearls. ‘But I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.’ ‘The glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp.’ ‘Into the city will be brought the glory and honor of the nations.’
21.big: The whole city is God’s dwelling place, and his people from Israel and the nations live in his presence.
21.diff: A cube. The Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple was a perfect cube (1 Kings 6:20). The whole city is now the place of God’s presence, so there is no temple. The measurements (12 x 1,000; walls of 144 cubits, 12 x 12) express completeness: the whole people of God, Old and New Testament together. Most interpreters read the city as a picture of the people of God (it is ‘the bride’) as well as their home.

22.ctx: Genesis 2 had a river and the tree of life; Ezekiel 47 a river flowing from the temple, with trees whose leaves are for healing.
22.mean: ‘A river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb’. On either side stands ‘a tree of life’, ‘And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations. No longer will there be any curse.’ ‘They will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads.’ ‘For the Lord God will shine on them, and they will reign forever and ever.’
22.big: Eden is restored and surpassed: the curse is gone and God’s people see his face.
22.diff: One throne belongs to ‘God and… the Lamb’, and ‘His servants will worship Him’: a single ‘Him’ for the two. Revelation never explains this, but it is the kind of language the church later expressed in the doctrine of the Trinity.

22.ctx: The book closes as it began (1:1–3), with a blessing on those who keep its words.
22.mean: ‘Behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of prophecy in this book.’ John again falls to worship the angel and is told, ‘Worship God!’ ‘Do not seal up the words of prophecy in this book, because the time is near.’ ‘I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End.’ ‘Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life’. ‘I, Jesus, have sent My angel’. ‘The Spirit and the bride say, “Come!”’ ‘And let the one who is thirsty come, and the one who desires the water of life drink freely.’
22.big: Jesus, the Alpha and Omega, is coming, and the invitation to come to him for the water of life is open to all.
22.diff: In verses 12–16 the same speaker calls himself ‘the Alpha and the Omega’ (God’s title in 1:8) and then says ‘I, Jesus’. ‘Soon’ has been waited for nearly 2,000 years; Christians have understood it as meaning the next great event in God’s plan, which could come at any time, so that every generation must be ready (compare 2 Peter 3:8–9).

22.h: Nothing May Be Added or Removed
22.ctx: Ancient authors sometimes ended books with a curse on anyone who changed them. Compare Deuteronomy 4:2.
22.mean: ‘If anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book. And if anyone takes away from the words of this book of prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and the holy city’. ‘He who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints. Amen.’
22.big: The Bible ends with a warning to handle God’s word faithfully, a promise, a prayer and grace.
22.diff: The warning concerns this book of prophecy in particular, though similar warnings appear in Deuteronomy 4:2 and Proverbs 30:6, and Christians have applied the principle to Scripture as a whole. It warns against both adding new ‘revelations’ and cutting out what is uncomfortable. ‘Come, Lord Jesus!’ is the Greek of the Aramaic prayer Marana tha (1 Corinthians 16:22).
